issues.legal_issue: A claimed error in the recorded area is not clerical when correcting it requires a later survey and would alter substantive rights in land covered by an acquisition.
material_facts: The acquisition award recorded that the land had been surveyed, checked, and approved, and described the whole of the disputed survey number as acquired.
The acquiring authority took possession of the whole survey number for a housing scheme.
The claimants initially asserted that some land had not been acquired without identifying its survey number, boundaries, or exact extent.
About 25 years later, the claimants sought a correction based on a new survey; the reported excess area differed from the extent they had originally claimed.
The original records did not show an arithmetical error, and determining the claimed error required a fresh survey.
issues.conclusion: The claimed change was not a clerical error eligible for correction under Section 87. The entire survey number had been acquired, and no part of it was left unacquired.
issues.legal_principle: Section 87 of the Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Land Revenue Act, 1317 Fasli permits correction of clerical errors. A clerical error is an accidental slip or omission that can be corrected without modifying a conscious adjudication or deciding a substantive issue; an arithmetical error is a mistake in calculation, and a clerical error is a mistake in writing or typing. The Court relied on M/s Tata Consulting Engineers v. Workmen, Sooraj Devi v. Pyare Lal, Master Construction Co. (P) Ltd. v. State of Orissa, and Vipinchandra Vadilal Bavishi (Dead) by Lrs. v. State of Gujarat. It distinguished the administrative circular’s example of a wrong area calculation because the alleged error here required a survey and resurvey. Administrative exposition under the principle discussed in K.P. Varghese v. Income Tax Officer and Desh Bandhu Gupta and Co. v. Delhi Stock Exchange Association Ltd. cannot prevail when it conflicts with the law laid down by the courts.

rule.if: land_acquisition_dispute and land_record_correction_proceeding and original_award_covers_entire_land_unit and possession_taken_over_entire_land_unit and correction_depends_on_later_resurvey and correction_would_change_substantive_acquisition_rights

predicates.land_acquisition_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether land was acquired through a land acquisition process.
predicates.land_record_correction_proceeding: A party seeks a correction to an official land record.
predicates.original_award_covers_entire_land_unit: The original acquisition award describes the whole relevant land unit as acquired.
predicates.possession_taken_over_entire_land_unit: The acquiring authority took possession of the whole relevant land unit.
predicates.correction_depends_on_later_resurvey: Establishing the alleged error requires a survey or resurvey after the original record was made.
predicates.correction_would_change_substantive_acqu: The proposed correction would affect which land or how much land is treated as acquired.

issues.definition: When a land-record correction in an acquisition dispute depends on a later resurvey and would alter substantive acquisition rights despite the original award and possession covering the whole land unit, the correction is not clerical.

issues.legal_issue: A power with no specified time limit must be exercised within a reasonable time, and an unexplained, prolonged delay is unreasonable where third-party interests have been created.
material_facts: The claimants applied to correct the land records about 25 years after the acquisition and possession had taken place.
They gave no explanation for waiting that long, despite having earlier asserted that some land had not been acquired.
A housing scheme had been developed on the disputed or surrounding land, creating third-party interests.
The claimants argued that the absence of a time limit for correcting clerical errors allowed a claim at any time; the Court found that the claim was not clerical in any event.
issues.conclusion: The claim was hopelessly delayed and could not be entertained; the creation of third-party interests reinforced that conclusion.
issues.legal_principle: Where no time limit is specified, a statutory power must be exercised within a reasonable period, assessed in light of the facts and surrounding circumstances. The Court relied on Collector v. P. Mangamma and State of Gujarat v. Patel Raghav Natha. It also relied on Joint Collector, Ranga Reddy District v. D. Narsing Rao, which explains that delayed exercises of power create uncertainty and should not unsettle third-party rights without cogent explanation, and Basanti Prasad v. Chairman, Bihar School Examination Board, concerning interference where third-party rights are likely to be affected.

rule.if: land_record_correction_proceeding and no_fixed_time_limit_applies and claim_made_after_prolonged_unexplained_delay and settled_third_party_interests_exist

predicates.land_record_correction_proceeding: A party seeks an administrative correction to a land record.
predicates.no_fixed_time_limit_applies: The governing process does not specify a fixed period for making the relevant claim.
predicates.claim_made_after_prolonged_unexplained_d: The claimant waits a prolonged period to apply and gives no cogent explanation for the delay.
predicates.settled_third_party_interests_exist: Rights or interests of third parties have arisen in the land during the delay.

issues.definition: If a land-record correction claim has no fixed filing limit but is made after a prolonged, unexplained delay and third-party interests have arisen, the claim is unreasonable and must be rejected.

issues.legal_issue: An entity whose land or project interests are directly affected by a correction proceeding has standing to challenge the adverse decision.
material_facts: The housing board acquired the disputed land and developed a housing scheme on it.
The requested correction would have treated part of the land as not acquired, threatening the board’s interests and those of the scheme’s beneficiaries.
The board participated in the administrative proceedings and challenged the adverse orders.
issues.conclusion: The housing board was directly and primarily affected by the claim and had standing to participate in and challenge the proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: An entity directly affected by a claim, and responsible for protecting the interests of persons who would be affected by the outcome, has standing to participate in proceedings and challenge an adverse order. The Court noted that the administrative authority had also directed that the board be heard before orders were made.

predicates.challenge_to_administrative_order: An entity seeks to participate in or challenge an administrative order concerning land.
predicates.challenged_claim_threatens_entity_land_o: The claim underlying the order threatens the entity’s land or project interests.
predicates.entity_responsible_for_protecting_affect: The entity is responsible for protecting the interests of people who would be affected by the claim.

issues.definition: An entity has standing to challenge an administrative order when the underlying claim threatens its land or project interests and it is responsible for protecting affected beneficiaries.

issues.legal_issue: A court may interfere with factual conclusions reached by revenue authorities when those authorities misdirect themselves in law and exercise jurisdiction they do not possess.
material_facts: Revenue authorities reopened a land-area issue that had been settled in connection with the original acquisition decades earlier.
They relied on later measurements to reach conclusions inconsistent with the claimants’ asserted extent and with a subsequent survey report.
The authorities treated the matter as a clerical correction even though deciding it required a resurvey and affected substantive acquisition rights.
issues.conclusion: The courts were not precluded from interfering with the revenue authorities’ factual conclusions because the authorities had misdirected themselves in law and exercised jurisdiction not vested in them.
issues.legal_principle: Factual conclusions are not insulated from judicial interference where the deciding authorities have misdirected themselves in law or exercised jurisdiction they do not possess. The Court applied this principle to the authorities’ reopening of a settled factual issue through a correction process that did not extend to the substantive dispute before them.

rule.if: judicial_review_of_revenue_decision and authority_reopened_settled_factual_issue and authority_misdirected_itself_in_law and authority_exceeded_its_jurisdiction

predicates.judicial_review_of_revenue_decision: A court is reviewing a decision made by a revenue authority.
predicates.authority_reopened_settled_factual_issue: The authority reconsidered a factual issue that had already been settled.
predicates.authority_misdirected_itself_in_law: The authority applied the law incorrectly to the issue before it.
predicates.authority_exceeded_its_jurisdiction: The authority exercised a power it did not possess.

issues.definition: When a revenue authority reopens a settled factual issue while misapplying the law and exceeding its jurisdiction, a reviewing court may interfere with its factual conclusion.
